sources.news_title: Republican officials order investigations of Peltola and other Democrats after New York Times report
sources.text:
Republican officials order investigations of Peltola and other Democrats after New York Times report
Carmella Warfield, chair of the Alaska Republican Party, and Gov. Mike Dunleavy listen to JD Vance deliver a speech at an Oct. 5, 2026, campaign rally in Fairbanks. Vance was in Alaska to campaign for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
Alaska’s governor said late Wednesday that he is ordering the Alaska Department of Public Safety to investigate whether Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola, her campaign or national Democratic groups violated state law by recruiting independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan to run in this year’s election.
Sullivan’s recruitment was first reported Wednesday by the New York Times, which said Democratic campaigners worked through an intermediary to convince Sullivan to run for office and act as a spoiler for Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan’s re-election campaign.
State law does not prohibit the recruitment of spoiler candidates, and it is a tactic that has been used by both Republicans and Democrats in statewide races within Alaska.
Alaska’s Senate race is thought to be among a handful of elections that may decide whether Republicans or Democrats control the Senate.
Following Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s announcement, a Republican member of the U.S. House said he would also investigate, and the Associated Press reported that the U.S. Department of Justice has expanded an ongoing criminal investigation.
Speaking Thursday on Fox News, Gov. Mike Dunleavy said the state investigated Sullivan’s candidacy before ruling him ineligible, a ruling that was overturned by the Alaska Supreme Court in June.
“With these new revelations in the New York Times article, we’re more than compelled to follow up on the investigation, and we are starting that diligently here today,” Dunleavy said.
Trump calls for Peltola to be criminally charged, removed from Alaska’s U.S. Senate race
On Thursday morning, the head of the U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, Rep. James Comer, R-Kentucky, said he would seek to interview two of the sources cited by the Times.
He asked Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager and a source for the Times’ reporting, to sit for a voluntary interview after Election Day. If she does not agree, he said in a letter, “we will be forced to evaluate the use of compulsory process.”
Comer sent a similar letter to Jerid Kurtz, a person whom the Times article said acted as an intermediary between Democratic campaign groups and Dan J. Sullivan.
The U.S. Department of Justice is pursuing a criminal investigation into Dan J. Sullivan and the Peltola campaign, and the Associated Press — citing an unidentified source — said the DOJ issued more subpoenas related to the investigation on Thursday.
In addition, the DOJ is pursuing a civil lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections.
President Donald Trump said last week that he ordered the lawsuit, which asks a federal judge to prohibit anyone but Dan S. Sullivan from being declared the winner of the Senate election.
On Thursday, the DOJ filed an amended legal complaint that puts the Times article at the center of the issue.
Judge Sharon Gleason — an appointee of President Barack Obama — had been expected to rule by Monday on motions seeking to dismiss the DOJ lawsuit, but hours after its filing, the DOJ argued that the amended complaint means she should push back her deadline.
That could mean a ruling on or after Election Day.

sources.news_title: Dunleavy calls for investigation into Democrats' reported ballot-stacking effort in Alaska U.S. Senate race
sources.text:
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation Wednesday into whether efforts by Democrats to recruit a same-name challenger to Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan violated state law.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that staff for Democrat Mary Peltola, who is challenging Sullivan, and other Democratic aides secretly pushed a retired Petersburg teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run against the incumbent senator in hopes of improving Peltola’s chances. Peltola has denied the allegation.
In a post on social media Wednesday evening, Dunleavy, a Republican, said the report represented “disturbing” evidence of an effort to “manipulate Alaska’s elections” to “deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.” He directed the state’s Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the “scheme” violated state law and whether criminal charges or civil penalties were warranted.
“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support,” he said. “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections.”
Dunleavy’s call for an investigation comes five days before Election Day, with early voting in Alaska already underway. It followed President Donald Trump’s demands that Peltola be criminally prosecuted. Trump, Dunleavy and Sen. Sullivan are close allies who campaigned together in Wasilla earlier this month. The Associated Press, citing an unnamed source, reported Thursday that the Justice Department had issued a number of new subpoenas and was preparing more in an ongoing investigation of the Petersburg Sullivan’s candidacy.
In his post, Dunleavy did not say what laws may have been broken or who the state’s investigation would target. Several legal experts said the facts outlined in the Times report did not appear to add up to a crime.
Dunleavy says revelations may be ‘tip of iceberg’
In an interview on Fox News, Dunleavy said the Petersburg Sullivan should not be on the ballot.
“We knew there was something going on there, but we’re also somewhat surprised by the revelations, and we now believe that that’s probably just the tip of the iceberg,” Dunleavy said.
He said state officials would be “following up on investigations and discussions” with Dan J. Sullivan.
The Petersburg Sullivan previously denied links to the Peltola campaign and hasn’t responded to inquiries since the publication of the Times story.
The Alaska Division of Elections initially sought to remove the Petersburg teacher from the ballot ahead of the August primary election, saying he had filed to run “for the purpose of confusing or misleading voters.” The Alaska Supreme Court rejected the claim and ordered he be placed on the ballot.
Then last week, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to block the certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Sen. Sullivan narrowly loses, saying Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy was intended to confuse voters and benefit Peltola.
The Alaska Bureau of Investigation will handle the probe ordered by Dunleavy, said Department of Public Safety spokesperson Austin McDaniel. He declined to say what the investigation would focus on.
“We recognize that Alaskans want and deserve fact-based answers surrounding these allegations, and we are committed to providing accurate information as the investigation progresses,” McDaniel said. “However, to protect the integrity of this active investigation, we are unable to provide additional details at this time.”’
‘Unsavory isn’t always illegal’
The vagueness of the governor’s announcement of an investigation is “peculiar,” said Scott Kendall, an Alaska attorney who once served as chief of staff for independent Gov. Bill Walker.
Democrats’ conduct outlined in the Times’ investigation was “sordid,” “gross” and “unethical,” Kendall said, but not necessarily criminal.
“The story lacks facts that would lead, in my mind, to criminal charges,” he said. “Unsavory isn’t always illegal.”
Others said they, too, were puzzled by the suggestion the findings added up to a violation of state law.
“I’m not aware of a state statute or regulation that would prohibit recruiting a candidate with a similar name to challenge another candidate on the Alaska ballot,” said John Lindback, former chief of staff to Alaska Lt. Gov. Fran Ulmer, a Democrat.
In 2024, a former Florida state senator and campaign consultant was convicted on felony charges for a scheme aimed at tipping a tight state legislative race that involved paying a “ghost candidate” with the same last name as the Democratic incumbent more than $44,000 in cash and gifts to run for the seat.
The fact that money changed hands makes the Florida case distinct from the Sullivan saga, Kendall said.
“If the state of Alaska had video of Decoy Dan being handed a paper bag with $100,000, we’re having a different conversation,” he said.
President Trump and a number of other Republican leaders have also called for an investigation into whether efforts to recruit a second Sullivan constituted federal crimes. But former Department of Justice attorney and Loyola Law School professor Justin Levitt said the facts brought to light by the Times report don’t appear to indicate a federal crime, either.
“The only thing I can think of is if — IF — there were an undisclosed payment made in service of Sullivan’s actual campaign (once he announced), that would run up against some campaign finance rules,” Levitt said. “But I haven’t heard of anything like that sort of payment, and just working to convince someone to run doesn’t violate any law I’m aware of.”
The chair of the U.S. House Oversight Committee, Kentucky Republican Rep. James Comer, said Thursday he’s requesting interviews with the aides identified by the Times as involved in the effort, Politico reported.

sources.news_title: Alaska allegations complicate fight for US Senate control
sources.text:
Alaska's Republican governor has ordered a state investigation of allegations in a New York Times report that Democrats recruited spoiler candidates in the state’s US Senate race.
The Times reported that aides to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola worked to recruit two candidates who could siphon votes from incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.
The allegations raise the prospect of a messy fight over a contest that could determine Senate control in next Tuesday's midterm elections.
Alaska is one of about 10 highly competitive races that will decide control of the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats, and a post-election dispute in Alaska could leave control of the chamber unclear for weeks.
Governor Mike Dunleavy said that the probe would examine whether any laws were broken, posting on X that "the evidence will determine what happens next".
President Donald Trump told reporters: "It's hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don't know how you can allow somebody like that to run. It's so unfair."
Mr Trump for years has sowed doubts about the fairness of US elections and even prior to the Times report had pushed the Justice Department to file a lawsuit seeking to pre-emptively block Alaska from certifying Ms Peltola, a former congresswoman, if she were to win the election.
The Times reported today that Peltola aides worked with campaign lawyers and staff at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to recruit two candidates who could siphon votes from the incumbent Republican Sullivan, including a retired teacher also named Dan Sullivan who is on the ballot.
Ms Peltola’s former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August, told the Times that Ms Peltola was aware of the effort.
Ms Peltola’s campaign said it "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign".
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee also denied involvement and accused Republicans of propping up candidates of their own in other races.
'Alaskans deserve the honest truth'
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, lambasted what he called the "crazy tactics" of Democrats in Alaska.
In an interview with Fox News, he said: "We hope it doesn't confuse voters, but that's exactly what the Democrats tried to do here.
"They got caught red-handed."
US Senator Lisa Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, called for Ms Peltola to be honest.
"Recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong," she posted on X.
"Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign - what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and cover-ups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials," she added.
Jessica Levinson, a professor who specialises in election law at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, said that as long as Daniel J Sullivan, the challenger to the incumbent, did not conceal financial support, his campaign likely did not break any laws and political parties are allowed to mislead the public.
Policing such behaviour would open the door to the government investigating why candidates choose to run and why voters support them, she said.
"To the extent that people are uncomfortable with two Sullivans, I would offer you're probably going to be uncomfortable with a really high level of government intrusion into our elections as well," she added.
Rex Van Middlesworth, an executive board member of Keep Our Republic, a nonpartisan group that works to build trust in US elections, said on a call with reporters that nothing would bar the second Sullivan from the ballot or disqualify Ms Peltola.
He called the Justice Department’s lawsuit "frivolous even by current DOJ standards", saying it cites no provision of law.

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy Orders Probe Into Mary Peltola Campaign Over Second Dan Sullivan on Ballot
Oct. 29 2026, Published 2:53 p.m. ET
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into whether Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign violated state law by helping recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
The Republican governor announced the probe Wednesday night, directing the Alaska Department of Public Safety to investigate after a New York Times report detailed an alleged effort involving people connected to Peltola's campaign and national Democrats.
The controversy comes just days before Alaska voters head to the polls in a Senate race that could help determine control of the chamber.
Dunleavy Cites Times Report On Ballot Plan
Dunleavy said the Times report provided new evidence of an effort to manipulate Alaska's elections by recruiting candidates with names similar to those of existing candidates.
"Today's New York Times reporting reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska's elections by recruiting candidates - including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator - to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes," Dunleavy wrote on social media.
He said the Alaska Division of Elections had already examined similar concerns and that the new reporting "substantially supports" its earlier findings.
"I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted," Dunleavy said. "The evidence will determine what happens next."
Dunleavy also said voters have a right to cast ballots for the candidate they intend to support.
Second Dan Sullivan at Center of Controversy
The dispute centers on Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, who is running against the incumbent senator.
Alaska's certified general-election ballot lists Dan S. Sullivan as a registered Republican and incumbent, while Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. is also listed as a registered Republican. Mary Peltola and Gerald Heikes are the other candidates on the regular ballot.
The Times reported, based on interviews, text messages, and documents, that a Democratic operative who worked with Peltola's campaign and national Democrats helped encourage Daniel J. Sullivan to enter the race.
The report described a broader effort to identify people named Dan Sullivan who could run against the incumbent.
Former Peltola campaign manager Elisa Rios also discussed the alleged effort with the Times before attempting to retract her interviews, according to the report.
Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has denied being recruited by Democrats and has maintained that he entered the race on his own.
Peltola Campaign Denies Role as Trump Weighs In
Peltola's campaign has denied involvement with either Sullivan campaign. During a campaign stop in Soldotna, she dismissed the controversy as a distraction.
"This is just another distraction. It's another diversion," Peltola said.
President Donald Trump has also called for Peltola to face prosecution. "I think they should be prosecuted," he said Wednesday, according to reports.
The Justice Department has separately sued to prevent certification of the election under certain circumstances if Dan Sullivan loses and voter confusion involving the two Sullivans is alleged to have affected the outcome.
Ballot Battle Heads to Election Day
The Alaska Supreme Court previously allowed Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to remain on the ballot after state election officials initially sought to remove him, arguing that his candidacy could confuse voters.
The court ruled that state election officials' authority was limited by the constitutional qualifications for candidates, clearing the way for Sullivan to run.
The controversy now heads into the Nov. 3 general election, with the state's ranked-choice voting system adding another layer to the closely watched Senate contest. The ballot distinguishes the two Sullivans by name, party affiliation, and incumbent status.
Dunleavy's investigation will determine whether the alleged recruitment effort violated Alaska law and whether further legal action is warranted.

President Trump addressed the story Wednesday at Joint Base Andrews before leaving to campaign for Republicans in Ohio. He said Peltola should leave the race and face prosecution.

Subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters in the hotly contested race.
More subpoenas were expected to be sent Thursday, according to a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the total number of them were immediately clear.
It’s the latest aggressive move by the Justice Department in a politically sensitive matter in the weeks leading up to Tuesday’s midterm elections. The Justice Department has historically avoided taking overt investigative actions against candidates in the weeks before an election, or other public steps that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
Election law experts said they were unaware of what federal law would justify the investigation.
“I don’t know what they’re putting out subpoenas to investigate because I don’t know what federal violations are implicated that DOJ would have jurisdiction over,” said Justin Levitt, a former Department of Justice official under President Joe Biden. “Sure makes it seem like the point of the investigation is to become the story.”

Earlier Thursday, a federal judge in California appointed a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that the state has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. That action came less than 24 hours after the judge rejected the Justice Department’s demand that California sequester the ballots until citizenship can be verified, a ruling the department immediately appealed.
For months, the Justice Department has been looking into allegations that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race to mislead voters and help Peltola’s campaign. The potential targets of the Justice Department’s investigation are unclear, but President Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign.

sources.news_title: Alaska's governor orders a probe into Peltola's Senate campaign over the second Sullivan candidate
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department is escalating a criminal investigation over an Alaska Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press on Thursday.
Subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters in the hotly contested race.
More subpoenas were expected to be sent Thursday, according to a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the total number of them were immediately clear.
It's the latest aggressive move by the Justice Department in a politically sensitive matter in the weeks leading up to Tuesday's midterm elections. The Justice Department has historically avoided taking overt investigative actions against candidates in the weeks before an election, or other public steps that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
Election law experts said they were unaware of what federal law would justify the investigation.
“I don’t know what they’re putting out subpoenas to investigate because I don’t know what federal violations are implicated that DOJ would have jurisdiction over,” said Justin Levitt, a former Department of Justice official under President Joe Biden. “Sure makes it seem like the point of the investigation is to become the story.”
The information came to light the same day that the U.S. Justice Department issued subpoenas to California officials in an escalation of its scrutiny of local election administration. Earlier Thursday, a federal judge in California appointed a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that the state has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. That action came less than 24 hours after the judge rejected the Justice Department’s demand that California sequester the ballots until citizenship can be verified, a ruling the department immediately appealed.
Race is among a handful that could determine control of the Senate
For months, the Justice Department has been looking into allegations that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race to mislead voters and help Peltola’s campaign. The potential targets of the Justice Department’s investigation are unclear, but President Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign.
The new subpoenas were confirmed by a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe.
Attorney General Todd Blanche in a Fox News interview on Wednesday said he wouldn’t discuss any criminal investigations, but accused Democrats of “cheating.”
“They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues but by putting up a person with the same name,” Blanche said.
The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
In an updated filing Thursday, the government said the details in the Times story contradicted statements given earlier by attorneys for Democrats and the Peltola campaign, in which they said they “lack knowledge” of how Dan J. Sullivan came to run for the office.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
Alaska's Republican governor has also ordered an investigation
Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper's reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections.”
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens," the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. "It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Later, as he rallied for GOP Sen. Darline Graham, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted."
Peltola dismisses the claims as a ‘distraction’
Peltola’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a message Thursday seeking comment on Dunleavy’s order. But during a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola, a former congresswoman, suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion,” she said in a video posted online. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which The New York Times' story alleges was involved in the effort to recruit the other Dan Sullivan, didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
The situation in Alaska isn't that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results.
In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.
On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as Trump did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud.
“I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.”
State Supreme Court OK'd the other Sullivan on the ballot
Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher, ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.
The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator.
Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.”
Meg Kinnard can be reached at http://x.com/MegKinnardAP. AP writers Seung Min Kim, Nicholas Riccardi and Ali Swenson contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: DOJ issues new subpoenas in Alaska election investigation
sources.text:
The Justice Department has issued a new round of grand jury subpoenas as it escalates a criminal investigation into allegations surrounding the recruitment of a candidate who shares a name with Republican Alaska Senator Dan Sullivan, according to the Associated Press.
The subpoenas seek grand jury testimony or documents, while records-preservation demands have also been issued, the AP reported Thursday, citing a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity. More subpoenas were expected Thursday, although the number of subpoenas and their recipients were not immediately clear.
The development represents a significant escalation of the controversy surrounding Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher who will appear on Tuesday's ballot alongside incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola.
Read More on News
The Justice Department has been investigating allegations that Sullivan Jr. entered the race to siphon votes from the incumbent, according to the AP. The latest subpoenas come after The New York Times reported that people working with Peltola's campaign and senior Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) aides participated in efforts to recruit Sullivan Jr. or other candidates who could draw support from the Republican senator. The newspaper cited interviews, text messages and other documents. Peltola's campaign and the DSCC have denied recruiting Sullivan Jr. or other candidates.
The Justice Department has not publicly disclosed what potential federal offenses it is examining.
The federal investigative development comes as Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy has separately directed the Alaska Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the alleged effort violated state law and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted.
The expanding state and federal investigations raise a key unanswered legal question: Even if political operatives deliberately encouraged Sullivan Jr. or other candidates to enter the race to draw votes from the incumbent, what criminal law, if any, would such conduct violate?
Jeff Feldman, a University of Washington law professor who has litigated extensively in Alaska, told Newsweek on Thursday that "it's less than clear that such conduct would violate any provision of Alaska law."
Feldman's comments addressed potential violations of Alaska law, rather than whatever federal theory prosecutors may be examining. The Justice Department has not publicly disclosed the legal basis for its criminal investigation.
Attempts to remove Sullivan Jr. from the ballot have already failed in state court. The Alaska Division of Elections concluded earlier this year that his candidacy was intended to confuse or mislead voters, but a judge reversed the decision after finding that Alaska law did not impose a "good faith" requirement on candidates. The Alaska Supreme Court subsequently allowed Sullivan Jr. to remain on the ballot.
The state, meanwhile, is fighting a separate Justice Department lawsuit over the same election. On October 26, Alaska's Department of Law asked a federal judge to dismiss the case, arguing against the federal government's legal basis for intervening in the state's administration of the race.
Newsweek has reached out to Peltola's campaign, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and the Justice Department for comment. The Alaska Department of Public Safety provided a statement confirming that the Alaska Bureau of Investigation has initiated an investigation.
DOJ Issues New Grand Jury Subpoenas
The new subpoenas add a criminal-investigation track to an already complicated legal fight. The Justice Department is separately pursuing a civil lawsuit seeking federal court intervention in the election, while Dunleavy has ordered a state investigation into whether Alaska law was violated.
The Justice Department has not publicly identified the potential targets of its criminal investigation or the potential federal offenses it is examining.
President Donald Trump has called for Peltola and her campaign to be prosecuted. Vice President JD Vance, however, stopped short Thursday of saying the conduct described in the reporting was criminal.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Vance said: "Whether it's criminal or not, she certainly has committed, I think, a great moral failing, and hopefully the voters of Alaska punish her."
Who Is the Other Dan Sullivan?
Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. is a retired teacher from Petersburg who is running alongside Peltola, incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan and Republican Gerald Heikes.
The two Sullivans are distinguished on the general-election ballot. The incumbent is identified as "Dan S. Sullivan (Registered Republican) Incumbent," while his challenger appears as "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr." without a party designation.
Sullivan Jr. has maintained that he entered the race of his own accord because he was dissatisfied with the incumbent's representation and wanted to offer Alaskans another choice.
But The New York Times reported on Wednesday that people working with Peltola's campaign and Democratic operatives were involved in a broader effort to find potential candidates who could draw support from the incumbent. According to the newspaper, a Peltola staffer was instructed in 2025 to search voter records for Alaskans named Dan Sullivan.
The Times said its reporting was based on interviews with 12 people who participated in or were told about the effort, or who were approached about running, as well as text messages and other documents.
Its reporting relied in part on former Peltola campaign manager Elisa Rios, who was fired in August. Rios initially provided extensive information about the alleged operation but sought to retract her statements before publication. The Times said her account was consistent with its other reporting.
Peltola's campaign has denied involvement, saying it "did not recruit any candidates into the race." The DSCC has also denied participating in efforts to recruit Sullivan Jr. or other candidates.
Mike Dunleavy Opens Investigation Into Peltola Campaign: What We Know
Dunleavy said on Wednesday that the Times reporting "substantially supports the Division's findings" and directed the Department of Public Safety to examine whether Alaska laws were violated and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted.
"Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections," Dunleavy said. "Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable."
Alaska Department of Public Safety Deputy Commissioner Austin McDaniel told Newsweek Thursday that the Alaska Bureau of Investigation has initiated an investigation into the alleged conduct described by the Times.
"The Alaska State Troopers are committed to the fair and impartial enforcement of Alaska's criminal laws, including those that protect the integrity of our elections," McDaniel said.
McDaniel said investigators would work with the Alaska Department of Law to examine the allegations, but that officials could not provide additional details in order to protect the integrity of the active investigation.
The investigation marks a new phase in the state dispute because the earlier proceedings focused on whether officials could exclude Sullivan Jr. from the ballot, not whether people involved in his alleged recruitment could face criminal or civil consequences.
Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom opened an inquiry on June 8, and Elections Director Carol Beecher removed Sullivan Jr. from the ballot on June 15 after finding that he had filed "with a purpose to confuse or mislead."
A Superior Court judge reversed that decision on June 26, concluding that Alaska law did not impose a good-faith requirement for candidates. The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the ruling on June 29, clearing the way for Sullivan Jr. to remain on the ballot.
The distinction is significant. The courts did not necessarily determine whether the Division of Elections' factual concerns about Sullivan Jr.'s candidacy were correct. Rather, the Superior Court found that the "good faith" requirement used to exclude him did not appear in the U.S. Constitution, Alaska statutes or the Division's implementing regulations. The Alaska Supreme Court summarily affirmed that result.
Dunleavy's investigation could therefore present a different question: whether conduct surrounding the alleged recruitment effort violated some other provision of Alaska law.
The investigation also leaves Alaska taking two seemingly different positions over the controversy.
The Trump administration's Justice Department has filed its own lawsuit over the election, seeking federal court intervention if Senator Sullivan loses under circumstances in which votes cast for Sullivan Jr. could have affected the result.
Alaska, however, has asked a federal judge to dismiss that case, arguing that Washington lacks the authority asserted by the Justice Department.
The positions are not necessarily inconsistent. Feldman told Newsweek that Alaska's arguments against the federal lawsuit would not affect or have "any obvious bearing" on a separate state investigation.
Could Recruiting a Candidate to Split Votes Be Illegal?
Neither the state nor federal authorities have publicly established that recruiting a candidate to draw votes from an opponent would, by itself, constitute a crime. What investigators would need to establish, and under which statutes, remains unclear.
Feldman pointed to AS 15.56.014, an Alaska statute that prohibits certain false campaign communications, but said it was unclear whether the conduct alleged here would fall within that law. He also noted that violations of Alaska's campaign-finance laws, contained in AS 15.13, can result in criminal prosecution but said there have been no allegations to date involving campaign-finance violations.
Feldman also said that none of the three grounds for contesting an election under AS 15.20.540 appears to fit the conduct alleged so far.
Those provisions cover misconduct, fraud or corruption by election officials sufficient to change the result; the legal qualifications of a person certified as elected; and legally defined "corrupt practices" sufficient to change the result. Feldman said no election-official misconduct has been alleged, no allegations appear to affect Peltola's legal qualifications for office, and the alleged conduct does not appear to fall within the "corrupt practices" defined by AS 15.56.030.
Political parties and their allies have previously supported candidates who could draw votes from opponents, and similar tactics have been employed by both major parties.
Alaska had another fight over an unconventional candidate two years ago. In 2024, the Alaska Democratic Party sued to remove Democratic U.S. House candidate Eric Hafner from the general-election ballot after two candidates who had finished ahead of him withdrew. Hafner was serving a federal prison sentence in New York.
The Alaska Republican Party intervened in the case on the side of the Division of Elections, arguing that Hafner should remain on the ballot. The dispute centered on whether Alaska's election law allowed the Division to successively replace more than one top-four primary finisher after withdrawals. The Alaska Supreme Court ultimately sided with the Division and allowed Hafner to remain on the ballot.
The circumstances differed from this year's Sullivan case, which centered on whether election officials could impose a "good faith" candidacy requirement. But the Hafner case shows that Alaska Republicans have previously intervened in litigation to keep an unconventional candidate on the ballot when Democrats sought his removal.
The Alaska courts have likewise rejected the state's attempt this year to exclude Sullivan Jr. because of his alleged motivation for running.
Feldman said the Alaska Supreme Court's ruling does not restrict the state's ability to investigate whether Alaska law was violated. While there is factual overlap between the earlier case and the new investigation, he said, "the legal issues they trigger are different."
The Justice Department's federal lawsuit presents still another legal issue, relying on federal law and arguing that potential voter confusion involving the two Sullivans could undermine the integrity of the election.
Feldman said Alaska's opposition to that federal lawsuit also would not prevent it from conducting its own investigation.
"The State makes several legal arguments in the federal court case, including a challenge to the standing of the federal government to raise the claims at all and whether the federal statute that the federal government relies on even applies in these circumstances," he said. "Those legal arguments would not be affected by or have any obvious bearing on an investigation."
Election-law experts have also questioned the legal basis for the Justice Department's federal case.
Michael Morley, the Sheila M. McDevitt professor of law and faculty director of the Election Law Center at Florida State University, previously told Newsweek that concerns about voter confusion could be legitimate while describing the DOJ lawsuit itself as "completely meritless."
"The DOJ's lawsuit is based on very real and valid concerns about voter confusion," Morley said. But he added that the department had sued under the National Voter Registration Act without alleging that the statute itself had been violated.
Mark Brown, a professor at Capital University Law School, previously told Newsweek that "no federal statute authorizes the relief the DOJ seeks" and called the lawsuit "frivolous."
Those comments concerned the Justice Department's civil lawsuit, rather than the separate criminal investigation in which the new subpoenas were issued.
Dan J. Sullivan Switches From Republican to Undeclared
Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. will enter the general election registered as an undeclared voter after switching his registration from Republican when he requested an absentee ballot for the August primary, according to records from the Alaska Division of Elections reported by the Alaska Beacon.
Sullivan Jr. was previously a member of the Alaska Independence Party and became a political independent after the party dissolved earlier this year. He switched his registration to Republican when he filed to run for the U.S. Senate.
But when he requested an absentee ballot ahead of the August primary, Sullivan listed his political affiliation as "undeclared," changing his registration again.
The distinction is notable in light of the controversy over his candidacy. Sullivan Jr.'s decision to register as a Republican when he filed was among the factors cited by the Division of Elections when it initially determined that he was not running in good faith.
His current registration is also reflected in how the two Sullivans are presented to voters.
Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. appears on the general-election ballot without a party affiliation beneath his name. The incumbent, by contrast, appears as "Dan S. Sullivan (Registered Republican) Incumbent."
There was also confusion over how Sullivan Jr.'s registration had changed.
When the Alaska Beacon initially contacted him about the switch, Sullivan Jr. said he had not requested it. Division of Elections spokesman Steve Kirch subsequently provided the outlet with a copy of Sullivan's absentee-ballot request showing that he had listed his affiliation as undeclared.
After being shown the document, Sullivan Jr. acknowledged the change.
"Holy cow...I did!" he told the Beacon. Sullivan added that he could "only guess" he had been thinking that because election officials did not give him a party affiliation on the ballot, "I should go with that," adding that he was "frazzled by all of this."
What Donald Trump Said About the Two Dan Sullivans
Trump has repeatedly intervened in the dispute and escalated his criticism after publication of the Times investigation.
Trump called for Peltola and Sullivan Jr. to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted, alleging that Democrats deliberately recruited the second Sullivan to deceive voters.
"They said they didn't do it, and they did do it, and they got caught," Trump told reporters on Wednesday, calling the alleged effort "voter fraud at the highest level."
Trump renewed his criticism on Thursday and left open whether Republicans should refuse to seat Peltola in the Senate in January if she wins the election.
Asked about doing so, Trump said: "Well, you're going to have to see what happens. It's hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don't know how you can allow somebody like that to run. It's so unfair."
Trump also renewed his argument that voters could confuse the two Sullivans.
"Most people would be inclined to vote for the Daniel, as opposed to the Dan, the way it sets up," he said. "It's very unfair, it's very confusing, and meant to be, it is a fraud."
Vice President JD Vance stopped short of agreeing that Peltola's reported conduct was criminal when asked about Trump's call for her prosecution.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Vance said: "Whether it's criminal or not, she certainly has committed, I think, a great moral failing, and hopefully the voters of Alaska punish her."
Trump has not identified a criminal statute that he believes was violated.
The president had already attacked Sullivan Jr.'s presence on the ballot before the Times investigation and took credit for the Justice Department lawsuit after it was filed.
"I'm the one that said 'do it,'" Trump told reporters last Friday.
Attorney General Todd Blanche subsequently defended the lawsuit while saying Justice Department lawyers had developed the case and that the department had not coordinated with a campaign or candidate.
The Justice Department's civil lawsuit and the criminal investigation that produced the new subpoenas are separate proceedings.
Have the Candidates Responded?
Peltola's campaign reiterated its denial of involvement after Dunleavy announced the investigation.
"Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any politician will keep her away from that fight," an Alaskans for Mary spokesperson told Newsweek on Thursday. "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."
Newsweek has asked Peltola's campaign whether the campaign or anyone working for it has received a federal grand jury subpoena, request for documents or records-preservation demand in connection with the investigation.
Sullivan Jr. has maintained that he entered the race independently because he was unhappy with Senator Sullivan's representation.
"It's a free country," he said after courts restored him to the ballot earlier this year, according to Courthouse News Service. "Most Alaskans are proud Independents and it's my sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but ultimately, choice is good and voters' intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running."
Senator Sullivan's campaign, however, has accused Peltola and her campaign of misleading voters about the alleged effort.
"Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along," spokesperson Nate Adams previously told Newsweek.
Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski has also criticized the conduct described in the Times report, saying "ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process."
But Murkowski has separately opposed the DOJ's lawsuit, arguing that Alaska has already distinguished between the two Sullivans on the ballot and saying the department "should never have filed" the case.
Mary Peltola vs. Dan Sullivan: What Latest Polls Show
Peltola holds a narrow advantage in VoteHub's polling average, which puts her at 49.8 percent to Sullivan's 47.1 percent, a 2.7-point lead.
A New York Times/Siena University poll conducted September 24-October 1 found Peltola ahead 50 percent to 43 percent among 504 likely voters.
An InsiderAdvantage poll conducted October 9-10 found Peltola leading 50 percent to 48 percent among 1,200 likely voters.
The close race has increased attention on the second Sullivan's candidacy. But Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, meaning voters can rank candidates in order of preference. If nobody wins a majority of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated and ballots cast for that candidate can transfer according to voters' subsequent choices.
Why Alaska Senate Race Matters in the 2026 Midterm Elections
The Alaska contest is among the Senate races that could help determine control of the chamber, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority.
Peltola, a former Alaska congresswoman, is seeking to become the state's first Democratic U.S. senator since Mark Begich was elected in 2008.
The increasingly bitter race now has several overlapping fronts: the campaign between Peltola and Senator Sullivan, allegations surrounding efforts to shape the four-person ballot, a federal criminal investigation, the Justice Department's separate civil lawsuit over the election and the state investigation ordered by Dunleavy.
Those proceedings pose distinct legal questions. The Justice Department has not publicly identified the potential targets or legal theory of its criminal investigation. Its civil lawsuit challenges the state's handling of the election, while Dunleavy's investigation is examining whether conduct surrounding the alleged recruitment effort violated Alaska law.
The courts have already concluded that election officials could not exclude Sullivan Jr. from the ballot under the rationale the state previously advanced.
The new subpoenas raise the stakes by showing that the controversy is now the subject of a federal criminal investigation involving grand jury process, even as it remains unclear who prosecutors are investigating or what potential violations they are examining.
Newsweek reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.

sources.news_title: Alaska Gov. orders probe of Peltola Senate campaign's alleged recruitment of 2nd Sullivan
sources.text:
The Department of Justice on Thursday escalated its lawsuit targeting potential certification of the result of Alaska's Senate election, which it argues could be tainted by the candidacy of a man with the same name as incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
The DOJ filed an amended version of its original complaint to add a new legal claim and to add details from Wednesday's New York Times article detailing alleged efforts by the people in the campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola to recruit a retired schoolteacher named Dan J. Sullivan into the race.
The amended complaint in Anchorage federal court suggests that Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee misled Judge Sharon Gleason by saying in recent court filings they lacked knowledge about why the retiree Sullivan entered the race earlier this year.
The amended suit also notes that Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, late Wednesday ordered the state Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the alleged recruitment of the retired teacher violated criminal or civil laws. Dunleavy cited the Times' report as the reason for that probe.
"The New York Times has reported that Alaskans For Mary and the DSCC were well aware of the purposes of Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy: they orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected," the DOJ said in its amended complaint.
The DOJ, in a separate filing Thursday, said that the filing of the amended complaint with the new claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution means that motions to dismiss the case by the state, Peltola's campaign, the DSCC and others are now moot. The DOJ cited precedent in the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals for that argument.
Gleason had given the DOJ until 5 p.m. Alaska Time Thursday to respond to the motions to dismiss, which have asked her to toss out the DOJ's original complaint before Election Day, Nov. 3.
The judge has yet to rule whether the dismissal motions are now moot. If she agrees with the DOJ, the parties could quickly file new motions to dismiss.
The DOJ's lawsuit, originally filed on Oct. 23, seeks to block the state from immediately certifying any Senate election result "that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the DOJ to file the suit.
The political stakes in the Alaska Senate race are potentially momentous. The winner could determine the power balance in the Senate, where Republicans hold a six-vote majority.
The new DOJ filings came as NBC News reported that the department "has issued at least three dozen new subpoenas and document preservation requests" to Peltola's campaign offices and those of the former schoolteacher Sullivan.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC, which have previously denied involvement in the retiree Sullivan's campaign to CNBC, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the amended DOJ suit.
Peltola's campaign, in a statement to CNBC on Thursday in response to Dunleavy's announcement, said, "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any politician will keep her away from that fight."
"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign," the campaign said.
Trump, before flying to South Carolina for a campaign rally Thursday morning, was asked by a reporter whether Senate Republicans should try to block Peltola from taking the seat in January if she wins Tuesday's election.
"Well, you're going to have to see what happens," Trump said.
"It's hard to believe that she can even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don't know how you can allow somebody like that to run," the president said.
Trump said the retired teacher Sullivan "was just put there as a fraud."
"But people aren't going to know that, so nobody's going to know what to do," Trump said.
Both Peltola's campaign and the DSCC have argued that Trump and other Republicans are being hypocritical in their claims about the Senate race.
"Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns — including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle," a DSCC spokesperson said Wednesday.

sources.text:
Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the Democratic candidate running for the U.S. Senate in the state after revelations that her campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting another candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
Dunleavy’s order, posted overnight on social media, comes a day after President Donald Trump called for the criminal prosecution of Mary Peltola and her campaign.
In a race that’s among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber, the Republican president had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of it, demanding that Alaska be prevented from certifying a win by Peltola if Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. remains on the state’s ballots.
Dunleavy wrote that reporting by The New York Times “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.”
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Peltola dismisses the claims as a ‘distraction’
Peltola’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a message early Thursday seeking comment on Dunleavy’s order. But during a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola, a former congresswoman, suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion,” she said in a video posted online. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as the president did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud.
“I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.”
State Supreme Court OK’d the other Sullivan on the ballot
Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg, ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. He has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign: “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.
The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator.
Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.” He earlier had posted on social media that “Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.”
Parties have backed other candidates before
While controversial, the situation in Alaska is not that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results. In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.

sources.text:
Alaska’s Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign following a report that her team helped recruit candidates to draw votes from her Republican opponent, including a man with the same name.
The announcement, posted on social media overnight, followed President Donald Trump’s call for Peltola’s prosecution and escalated Republican efforts to challenge her candidacy just days before an election that could help determine control of the Senate.
On Thursday, Trump declined to say whether Peltola should be seated if she won. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” he told reporters before leaving for a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Peltola is challenging Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan in the Nov. 3 election. Another candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, has denied running at Democrats’ behest. Alaska’s Supreme Court upheld his eligibility for the ballot earlier this year.
The dispute intensified Wednesday after a New York Times report found that Peltola's team worked with people to recruit men named Dan Sullivan to run for Senate, as well as other candidates who could draw votes away from the incumbent.
Dunleavy said the reporting provided new evidence of an effort to mislead voters and supported state election officials’ earlier findings about Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy.
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” the governor wrote.
Peltola, a former congresswoman, dismissed the report, arguing that it diverted attention from issues including the incumbent Sullivan’s support for the war in Iran.
“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion,” she said during a campaign stop in Soldotna on Wednesday. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
A spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign, Alaskans for Mary, said in an email to TIME that it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” The campaign also said it had made no assertions in federal court about how Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy came about or who was involved in his decision to run. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), which was also reportedly involved in the plan, told TIME in a statement that it was “not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.”
Vice President JD Vance also backed an investigation Thursday, accusing Peltola of trying to mislead voters about her campaign’s involvement. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful,” he told reporters before a campaign trip to Texas.
Trump had accused Peltola and her campaign of voter fraud in a series of Truth Social posts Wednesday, calling for her removal from the ballot and prosecution.
“It was just determined that the Dumocrats in Alaska, despite their sworn statements to the contrary, put a man named Dan Sullivan on the Ballot in order to confuse the Public with respect to Highly Esteemed Senator Dan Sullivan,” Trump posted. “This is Voter Fraud at the Highest Level, and the Dumocrat Candidate, who was involved in the scheme, Mary Peltola, should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted—So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan. Nothing else will do!”
The Times noted that ballot-stacking tactics are generally considered legal and have been used by both parties.
At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department had already filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the election results under specific conditions if Senator Sullivan loses, citing the potential for “voter confusion.” The department wants the results recalculated as though votes for Daniel J. Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, and certification blocked if that would change the outcome.
TIME reached out to the Justice Department for comment on how the report affects its case. Attorney General Todd Blanche told Fox News on Wednesday that he expected to “hear more” from the department this week as officials receive new information.
“They are cheating,” Blanche said. “They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues, but by putting up a person with the same name, so that confuses Alaskans.”
What Peltola’s campaign reportedly did
According to the Times’ report, which was based on interviews, text messages, and documents prepared for a possible lawsuit, the Peltola campaign pursued a project known internally as “ballot composition,” which involved campaign lawyers and senior aides at the DSCC, which directs Democratic campaign strategy for Senate races nationwide.
One of the Times’ sources, Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who was fired during an August staff shake-up, said the operation to recruit potential spoiler candidates for the Alaska ballot began in the summer of 2025. The Times reported that Peltola’s campaign worked with a “veteran Democratic operative” named Jerid Kurtz, whom it described as having expertise in ballot maneuvering.
The Times reported that a Peltola staffer received instructions to “find as many people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska” as possible. Kurtz reportedly found a man in Petersburg named Dan Sullivan who was open to running for Senate.
Rios said Peltola wasn’t directly involved in the project but was “definitely aware.” The Times also reported that Rios later wanted to recant her statements but did not explain why.
Alaska has a nonpartisan primary system, in which voters may choose a candidate regardless of party affiliation, and the top four advance to the general election. Voters then rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins an initial majority, the lowest-ranking candidates are eliminated in successive rounds and their ballots transfer to voters’ next remaining choices.
The spoiler candidate tactic isn’t new
Alaska’s other Senator, Lisa Murkowski, who endorsed Sullivan but supported Peltola years ago, issued a statement Wednesday demanding that Peltola tell the “honest truth” about the apparent ballot-stacking effort.
“While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process,” Murkowski wrote. “Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments. By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong.”
Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sullivan’s campaign, also said in a statement that “not one player in this operation has acted in good faith with Alaska voters.”
Republicans have also used similar ballot-stacking tactics. In this year’s Alaska primary, a GOP-aligned political action committee reportedly spent money to boost left-leaning fringe candidates in an attempt to pull votes from Peltola.
When Peltola ran for re-election to the House in 2024, Alaska’s Republican Party supported an effort to help a federally imprisoned Democrat who had never lived in Alaska stay on the ballot.
A GOP-linked political action committee also spent over $1 million this election cycle to boost a third-party candidate in Ohio in a bid to undermine former Senator Sherrod Brown’s comeback bid.
In Minnesota in 2020, Legal Marijuana Now Party candidate Adam Weeks told a close friend before his death that he was recruited by unnamed Republicans to pull votes away from Democrats.

Subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters in the hotly contested race.
More subpoenas were expected to be sent Thursday, according to a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the total number of them were immediately clear.
It’s the latest aggressive move by the Justice Department in a politically sensitive matter in the weeks leading up to Tuesday’s midterm elections. The Justice Department has historically avoided taking overt investigative actions against candidates in the weeks before an election, or other public steps that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
Election law experts said they were unaware of what federal law would justify the investigation.
“I don’t know what they’re putting out subpoenas to investigate because I don’t know what federal violations are implicated that DOJ would have jurisdiction over,” said Justin Levitt, a former Department of Justice official under President Joe Biden. “Sure makes it seem like the point of the investigation is to become the story.”
The information came to light the same day that the U.S. Justice Department issued subpoenas to California officials in an escalation of its scrutiny of local election administration. Earlier Thursday, a federal judge in California appointed a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that the state has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. That action came less than 24 hours after the judge rejected the Justice Department’s demand that California sequester the ballots until citizenship can be verified, a ruling the department immediately appealed.
Race is among a handful that could determine control of the Senate
For months, the Justice Department has been looking into allegations that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race to mislead voters and help Peltola’s campaign. The potential targets of the Justice Department’s investigation are unclear, but President Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign.
The new subpoenas were confirmed by a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe.
Attorney General Todd Blanche in a Fox News interview on Wednesday said he wouldn’t discuss any criminal investigations, but accused Democrats of “cheating.”
“They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues but by putting up a person with the same name,” Blanche said.
The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
In an updated filing Thursday, the government said the details in the Times story contradicted statements given earlier by attorneys for Democrats and the Peltola campaign, in which they said they “lack knowledge” of how Dan J. Sullivan came to run for the office.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
Alaska’s Republican governor has also ordered an investigation
Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper’s reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections.”
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Later, as he rallied for GOP Sen. Darline Graham, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.”
Peltola dismisses the claims as a ‘distraction’
Peltola’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a message Thursday seeking comment on Dunleavy’s order. But during a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola, a former congresswoman, suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion,” she said in a video posted online. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which The New York Times’ story alleges was involved in the effort to recruit the other Dan Sullivan, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The situation in Alaska isn’t that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results.
In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.
On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as Trump did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud.
“I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.”
State Supreme Court OK’d the other Sullivan on the ballot
Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher, ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.
The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator.
Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.”
