Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered a state investigation into allegations that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign helped recruit another candidate named Dan Sullivan to potentially divert votes from Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan in the November midterm elections.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
ANCHORAGE, Alaska — Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has directed state law enforcement officials to investigate allegations that Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign participated in an effort to recruit candidates intended to confuse voters and undermine Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan’s reelection campaign.
The investigation, announced Wednesday night, Oct. 28, follows a New York Times report alleging that individuals associated with Peltola’s campaign and Democratic political organizations helped recruit a retired schoolteacher named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to enter the Senate race against incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
According to The Associated Press, Dunleavy directed the Alaska Department of Public Safety to determine whether the alleged recruitment effort violated state election laws and whether criminal charges or civil proceedings are warranted.
The governor said the newspaper’s findings provided additional evidence supporting concerns previously raised by Alaska election officials.
Dunleavy wrote that the reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.”
He emphasized that voters must be able to identify their preferred candidates without deliberate interference.
“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support,” Dunleavy said. “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections.”
The governor said the state investigation would examine whether any individuals or organizations violated Alaska law.
The allegations center on Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, who qualified to appear on the November ballot despite objections from state election administrators.
He shares the first and last names of the Republican incumbent, creating concerns that some voters could inadvertently select the wrong candidate.
The New York Times investigation, described by CBS News, relied on interviews, text messages and documents prepared for potential litigation. The material reportedly indicated that individuals connected to Peltola’s campaign sought to encourage additional candidates to enter the race, potentially dividing support that otherwise might have gone to the incumbent senator.
Such political activity is sometimes referred to as ballot stacking or candidate recruitment. Encouraging candidates to run is not inherently illegal, but election officials and investigators may examine whether particular conduct involved fraud, misrepresentation or other violations.
The dispute began months before Dunleavy’s announcement.
In June, Alaska Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher determined that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. should not appear on the primary ballot, concluding that his candidacy had been filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The candidate challenged the determination, and the Alaska Supreme Court subsequently ruled that he was legally qualified to run.
The decision permitted his name to remain on the ballot despite objections concerning the potential for voter confusion.
Sullivan Jr. has repeatedly denied entering the election at the request of Democrats or coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
Asked in June whether he had communicated with the campaign, he responded, “Zero, none, zilch.”
His name appears on the general election ballot alongside the incumbent Republican, Peltola and another candidate.
Election materials distinguish the two Sullivans by identifying the incumbent as “Dan S. Sullivan,” a registered Republican and sitting senator, while listing the other candidate as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” without a party affiliation.
The allegations have prompted legal action beyond the state investigation.
The Trump administration previously filed a federal lawsuit seeking to prevent certification of the Alaska Senate election under certain circumstances if the similarly named candidate remained on the ballot.
The Justice Department argued that voter confusion could affect the election and sought judicial intervention to address the potential consequences.
According to CBS News, Attorney General Todd Blanche characterized the federal action as an effort to establish safeguards protecting the election process.
President Donald Trump confirmed his involvement in directing the federal lawsuit.
Asked about the case, Trump told reporters, “Well, I’m the one that said, ‘Do it.’”
Following publication of the New York Times investigation, the president called for criminal prosecution of Peltola and individuals associated with her campaign.
“I think they should be prosecuted,” Trump said Wednesday.
He also called for Peltola to face legal and political consequences over the allegations.
The former congresswoman and her campaign have denied involvement in recruiting the second Sullivan.
A campaign spokesperson said Peltola’s organization “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee also denied participating in the candidate’s recruitment.
A spokesperson for the organization said it “is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan,” while accusing Republicans of having previously supported candidates intended to divide opposition votes in other elections.
Peltola addressed the allegations during a campaign appearance in Soldotna, dismissing the newspaper’s investigation as an attempt to divert public attention from substantive political issues.
“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion,” Peltola said. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
She argued that voters should instead focus on policy disagreements, including Sullivan’s support for the war involving Iran.
Peltola’s campaign said the former congresswoman entered the race to address economic concerns and represent Alaska residents, rejecting suggestions that political pressure would force her to withdraw.
The dispute has become a prominent issue in Alaska’s Senate election, which is receiving national attention because of its potential implications for control of Congress.
Sullivan is seeking another term in the Senate, while Peltola is attempting to return to federal office after previously representing Alaska in the U.S. House.
The state’s election system allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference, adding another dimension to concerns about similarly named contenders.
Under ranked-choice voting, voters may select multiple candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the lowest-ranked candidates are eliminated in successive rounds, with votes transferred according to voters’ subsequent preferences.
The system makes it particularly important that voters accurately distinguish between candidates with similar names.
The New York Times findings have prompted competing interpretations of the recruitment effort.
Republican officials argue that placing a similarly named candidate on the ballot could intentionally misdirect voters and undermine confidence in the election.
Democrats deny coordinating the candidacy and have argued that allegations of wrongdoing remain unproven.
The Juneau Independent reported that recruiting additional candidates is a recognized political practice and is generally lawful, although specific conduct may raise legal questions depending on how recruitment occurs.
Dunleavy’s investigation will therefore examine whether the alleged activities crossed any legal boundaries rather than simply whether political operatives encouraged another person to run.
As of Thursday, Oct. 29, no criminal charges had been announced against Peltola or members of her campaign in connection with the allegations.
The Alaska Supreme Court’s earlier decision allowing Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to run remains significant because it established his eligibility for the ballot, although it did not resolve every allegation concerning the circumstances of his candidacy.
Dunleavy has said the evidence uncovered by state investigators will determine whether prosecutors or other authorities pursue further action.
With the Nov. 3 election approaching, the controversy has placed additional scrutiny on Alaska’s ballot procedures, campaign practices and the legal standards governing political efforts to influence voter choices.

When Democrats cannot win on the merits they rewrite the rules. That is the only conclusion left after a New York Times report detailed how operatives tied to Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign spent months hunting for another Alaskan named Dan Sullivan so they could plant him on the ballot and siphon votes from the Republican incumbent.
Governor Mike Dunleavy responded the only way a serious executive should. He ordered the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the scheme broke Alaska law and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted.
“Today’s New York Times reporting reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes,” Dunleavy wrote on X. “The Alaska Division of Elections investigated these very concerns in June of this year. The new reporting substantially supports the Division’s findings.”
He added that Alaskans “have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support” and that deliberately tricking voters “strikes at the integrity of our elections.”
The Times account is not subtle. In the summer of 2025 a Peltola staffer received instructions from top campaign aides to scour voter records for every person in the state named Dan Sullivan. The goal was obvious. Alaska’s ranked-choice system advances the top four finishers from the primary regardless of party. Planting a namesake next to Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan would force some voters to choose between two nearly identical names. The plan worked. A retired teacher from the tiny Panhandle village of Petersburg, Dan J. Sullivan, filed and made the general-election ballot.
The reporting goes further. The effort, internally called the “ballot composition project,” involved Peltola’s team, campaign lawyers, and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. Veteran operative Jerid Kurtz, described as a specialist in secret ballot maneuvers, made contact with the Petersburg Sullivan.
According to the Times, Kurtz told Peltola aides that the retiree “said he hated Trump, and if it was going to help Mary, he liked Mary.” Text messages show Peltola’s then-chief of staff worrying that Kurtz was being too conspicuous; a DSCC official replied they would “check in.”
Former campaign manager Elisa Rios, who was later fired, told the paper that Peltola herself was “definitely aware” of the operation even if she did not participate directly. Rios later tried to retract those statements. The Times said other evidence still supported the story.
Both the Peltola campaign and the DSCC continue to deny any role. “The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and did not recruit any candidates into the race,” the campaign told the Times. That denial now sits next to text messages, a dozen interviews, and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit.
In June the Division of Elections had already removed Dan J. Sullivan from the primary ballot after finding a “preponderance of the evidence” that his name and party affiliation were chosen to confuse voters. The Alaska Supreme Court put him back, ruling that state law does not require candidates to run in good faith. He appears on the November ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., listed without party affiliation, while the incumbent is clearly marked as the Republican.
President Trump called the scheme “Voter Fraud at the Highest Level” and demanded that Peltola be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.
“The Democrats cheated,” he wrote. “They found a man named Dan Sullivan, put him on the Ballot, then lied to the Court, and said they didn’t know anything about it. That’s perjury.”
Sen. Dan Sullivan, appearing on Hannity, said this is what happens when a candidate “has nothing to run on” and noted that Peltola still has not apologized. “What’s remarkable here is that even today, she has not apologized. Even today, she’s kind of playing as if nothing happened.”
The Justice Department has already sued to delay certification if the namesake’s votes could change the outcome.
Peltola dismissed the entire story as “all stuff to sell newspapers.” That is the classic response when the facts become inconvenient. Ballot-stacking is not new in Alaska, and both parties have used it. The difference is the months of public denial while the evidence of coordination accumulated.
Scripture does not grade on a curve when it comes to deliberate deception. “Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another” (Ephesians 4:25).
Voters are not pawns in a consultant’s game. They are citizens entitled to a clear choice between the candidates who actually want the job.
Dunleavy’s investigation will test whether Alaska’s laws can still reach an organized effort to confuse the electorate. The evidence will decide what comes next. Until then the rest of the country has a clear picture of how far some Democrats will go when the polling does not cooperate.
Two Storms, One Harvest
Every food crisis in living memory has been a one-shock event. The 2008 price spike was a commodity bubble. The 2020 shortages were a logistics failure. The 2022 grain scare was a war on one exporter’s ports. Each time, the system bent, adjusted, and recovered, and each time the experts assured us afterward that global markets are simply too big and too diversified to fail.
What nobody in Washington seems eager to discuss is that 2026 is shaping up to be something the modern food system has never actually faced. Two independent shocks, one climatic and one geopolitical, are converging on the same harvest cycle at the same time. Not sequentially. Simultaneously.
Start with the weather. The Pacific Ocean is currently building toward what forecasters now openly call a record event. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center puts the odds of at least a strong El Niño near 88 percent, with roughly two in three odds it reaches “very strong” status, the tier reserved for perhaps three or four events in the entire satellite era. Every major global model now projects a median peak in Super El Niño territory, and most of them project it exceeding the 2015-16 event, which until now held the modern record. Sea surface anomalies were already brushing the super threshold in mid-July, months before these events normally peak. The atmosphere has already shifted into El Niño mode, and the event is forecast to crest in late fall and early winter.
This is not about “climate change.” It’s about the standard cycles of weather, and the cycle we’re currently in is one that has likely devastated societies in the past. We’re better prepared as a society today, but not all Americans are equally prepared.
Serious households have started doing the quiet math on their own. Grocery bills tell part of the story, and the forecast maps tell the rest, which is why long-term food storage has moved from fringe hobby to mainstream line item in the family budget, with established suppliers like Heaven’s Harvest seeing demand from people who five years ago would have rolled their eyes at the idea. That instinct is not paranoia. It is pattern recognition, and the pattern is worth walking through carefully.

The Fertilizer Clock Is Already Running
While the Pacific warms, the second shock has been unfolding in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict with Iran turned the world’s most important energy chokepoint into a contested waterway, and the consequences reach far beyond the gas pump. Roughly a third of global fertilizer trade moves through Hormuz, and the disruption sent urea prices up 86 percent year over year by March, with a 53 percent jump in a single month.
The World Bank projects energy prices rising about 24 percent in 2026 and fertilizer about 31 percent. By its own accounting, fertilizer prices ran 35 percent higher in the first five months of this year than the same period last year.
Here is the mechanism the nightly news will not explain. Fertilizer is not a grocery item. It is a time-delayed input. The nitrogen a farmer in Iowa or Punjab could not afford to apply this spring does not show up as a problem this spring. It shows up as a thinner harvest six to twelve months later.
The World Bank’s own food security brief concedes that the effects of reduced applications earlier this season “are likely to become visible only later in harvest outcomes.” Translate that from institutional language into plain English and it means this. WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department is escalating a criminal investigation over an Alaska Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press on Thursday.
Subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters in the hotly contested race.
More subpoenas were expected to be sent Thursday, according to a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the total number of them were immediately clear.
It’s the latest aggressive move by the Justice Department in a politically sensitive matter in the weeks leading up to Tuesday’s midterm elections. The Justice Department has historically avoided taking overt investigative actions against candidates in the weeks before an election, or other public steps that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
Election law experts said they were unaware of what federal law would justify the investigation.
“I don’t know what they’re putting out subpoenas to investigate because I don’t know what federal violations are implicated that DOJ would have jurisdiction over,” said Justin Levitt, a former Department of Justice official under President Joe Biden. “Sure makes it seem like the point of the investigation is to become the story.”
The information came to light the same day that the U.S. Justice Department issued subpoenas to California officials in an escalation of its scrutiny of local election administration. Earlier Thursday, a federal judge in California appointed a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that the state has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. That action came less than 24 hours after the judge rejected the Justice Department’s demand that California sequester the ballots until citizenship can be verified, a ruling the department immediately appealed.
Race is among a handful that could determine control of the Senate
For months, the Justice Department has been looking into allegations that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race to mislead voters and help Peltola’s campaign. The potential targets of the Justice Department’s investigation are unclear, but President Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign.
The new subpoenas were confirmed by a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe.
Attorney General Todd Blanche in a Fox News interview on Wednesday said he wouldn’t discuss any criminal investigations, but accused Democrats of “cheating.”
“They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues but by putting up a person with the same name,” Blanche said.
The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
In an updated filing Thursday, the government said the details in the Times story contradicted statements given earlier by attorneys for Democrats and the Peltola campaign, in which they said they “lack knowledge” of how Dan J. Sullivan came to run for the office.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
Alaska’s Republican governor has also ordered an investigation
Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper’s reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections.”
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Later, as he rallied for GOP Sen. Darline Graham, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.”
Peltola dismisses the claims as a ‘distraction’
Peltola’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a message Thursday seeking comment on Dunleavy’s order. But during a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola, a former congresswoman, suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion,” she said in a video posted online. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which The New York Times’ story alleges was involved in the effort to recruit the other Dan Sullivan, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The situation in Alaska isn’t that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results.
In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.
On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as Trump did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud.
“I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.”
State Supreme Court OK’d the other Sullivan on the ballot
Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher, ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.
The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator.
Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.”
___

Peltola's campaign and the Democrats' Senate campaign arm have strongly denied any hand in getting the duplicate Sullivan on the ballot.
At a campaign stop in Soldotna, Alaska, Peltola called the report a "distraction," according to Alaska Public Media.
"Nobody's waking up worried about ballot composition," she said. "Not even me. I'm worried about my bills. I'm worried about affordability in health care."

On the campaign trail
• Red state events canceled: President Donald Trump will no longer headline a rally Sunday in Iowa, sources told CNN. He also scrapped plans for a Saturday event in deep-red Kansas and is instead planning as many as 20 telerallies before Election Day, officials said. Meanwhile, some GOP officials have expressed relief at the canceled rallies. “He hasn’t moved the needle anywhere,” one told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity.
• Democrats’ hopes soar: The forecaster “Inside Elections” has shifted 63 races in Democrats’ favor this week. Optimism is rising within the party that it can seize a Senate majority, and new CNN polling shows Democratic candidates leading in Michigan and Texas.
• Legal challenge: The Justice Department refiled a lawsuit seeking to block the potential results of Alaska’s Senate race as it conducts a criminal probe into whether state Democrats sought to confuse voters by stacking the ballot.
Updates
(57)
Republicans rush to capitalize on Times story about Alaska spoiler candidate
Republicans are scrambling to capitalize on Wednesday’s report from The New York Times that Democratic operatives affiliated with Alaska Senate hopeful Mary Peltola helped recruit a spoiler candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent.
The story arrived six days before the midterm election, leaving little time to produce and air ads highlighting the controversy. Meta, for example, has already stopped accepting new political ads for the election.
GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan has sought to draw awareness to the story through a series of TV appearances, including multiple interviews on Fox News and Newsmax. Sullivan’s campaign and the National Republican Senatorial Committee released videos attacking Peltola over the story, though it was unclear if they were paying to run them anywhere.
One super PAC supporting Sullivan, We Stand With Dan PAC, launched a radio ad Thursday telling listeners that the Times “just published an explosive story.”
“[Democrats] packed and funded the ranked-choice ballot against Sen. Dan Sullivan,” a narrator says in the minute-long spot. “The New York Times just put an exclamation point on a Peltola campaign built on lies. Shame on you, Mary Peltola.”
Peltola’s campaign has continued to deny involvement in the efforts described in the Times story.
"Both sides are doing it": Alaskans say Senate race controversy won’t affect their vote
Several voters at a crowded polling center in Anchorage’s midtown neighborhood told CNN the controversy surrounding Alaska’s Senate race is not influencing who they are voting for.
The Justice Department has dramatically accelerated a criminal probe into whether Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting a Senate candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, after a report by The New York Times described an alleged coordinated effort linked to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign.
Another independent voter, 50-year-old Jay Taylor who said he was “not a Trumper,” agreed, saying the controversy has gotten “way out of proportion” and argued that “the average Alaskan already knows who they are voting for.”
Election officials said they have seen long lines since the beginning of the early voting window last week, as Alaskans turn out to vote in a race that could decide the balance of power in the Senate.
Some GOP officials express relief at Trump's decision to cancel 2 weekend campaign visits
There’s little doubt President Donald Trump would have drawn large crowds during weekend campaign visits to Kansas and Iowa, given his popularity among the MAGA faithful, but some top Republican operatives in both states quietly expressed a sigh of relief at the canceled rallies.
A second Republican official said the Trump rallies were too time-consuming during a peak period when GOP activists would otherwise be door-knocking, canvassing and doing other get-out-the-vote activities.
The president has visited nearly every state on the Senate battleground map aside from Maine – many more than once. The White House decision to cancel the Midwest appearances was causing a tremendous amount of buzz, but few complaints among party stalwarts.
What's on the line for Elon Musk in the midterm elections
Billionaire Elon Musk has been a mega-donor in the midterms, as he and groups aligned with President Donald Trump are putting tens of millions of dollars into races to help Republicans.
Ronan Farrow, an investigative reporter and contributing writer at The New Yorker, explains what’s at stake for the world’s richest man.
Talarico criticizes AI-powered robocall push in final days of campaign
Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, who is running in Texas against GOP nominee Ken Paxton, responded to a recent push of AI-powered robocalls attacking his campaign, saying it is “pretty rich that they are using AI bots to attack me over data centers.”
The robocall campaign is powered by Lone Star Liberty, a pro-Ken Paxton super PAC that received $10 million from Elon Musk, which is looking to target Talarico for allegedly taking money from “data center special interest” groups, audio recordings reviewed by CNN show.
Talarico said he has criticized data centers that don’t “meet the demands of the people who live in these communities.”
CNN has reached out to Paxton for comment about the campaign.
Long lines ahead of rally for Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed
Long lines of voters twist outside of a rally in Kalamazoo, Michigan, for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as he makes his final push before the midterm election.
New CNN polling shows him having a 7-point lead over Republican Mike Rogers, but El-Sayed said earlier in the day “we’re going to run like we’re 10 points down.”
Trump scraps another rally, this one in Iowa, in strategy shift days before midterms
President Donald Trump is calling off a second planned rally for this weekend as he shifts strategy days before the midterm elections, two sources familiar with the matter said.
Trump will no longer headline a rally in Dubuque, Iowa, that was scheduled for Sunday, the sources said. Earlier Thursday, he had called off a separate rally in Kansas.
Instead, the president is planning as many as 20 telerallies in the days before Tuesday, hoping to maximize his presence in competitive districts where Republicans are running in close races, officials said.
CNN's Manu Raju reports from Iowa where polls indicate that the reliably red state has shifted to battleground territory. Democratic nominee Josh Turek is looking to defeat Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson in the race for the US Senate, while Democratic nominee Rob Sand and Republican nominee Zach Lahn are vying to be governor of Iowa.
For now, the only in-person event Trump has planned ahead of Tuesday is a rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday.
Officials said he is expected to spend Tuesday evening at the White House as results come it.
Democratic super PAC investing $750k into incredibly tight South Carolina Senate race
A Democratic super PAC will spend $750,000 on digital advertising to support Annie Andrews in the final days of the South Carolina Senate race.
Specifically, the digital ads will focus on “Graham raising healthcare costs” and drug prices, French posted on X.
Recent polling shows the race has tightened into a virtual tie in a state that few expected to be competitive at the beginning of the cycle.
A New York Times/Siena poll shows Andrews leading 57%-37% among independents and even pulls 7% of Republican likely voters. Some Republicans have expressed concerns about Graham’s lack of experience.
DOJ refiles lawsuit seeking to block results if GOP Sen. Sullivan loses in Alaska
The Justice Department has filed a revamped version of its lawsuit seeking to potentially block the certification of Alaska’s Senate election, coming on the heels of a New York Times report documenting Democratic efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan as a Republican candidate in the race, where the incumbent defending his seat is GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
In the new version of the federal lawsuit, DOJ alleges that the campaign of former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate nominee, and a national Democratic Party office submitted “misleading” arguments about their knowledge of the alleged efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan. To that point, it cites 12 different excerpts from the Times report.
Alaska election officials sought to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot earlier this year because they believed he was not running for the seat “in good faith.” The state Supreme Court later restored him to the ballot.
DOJ’s latest complaint says there is a “substantial likelihood” that his inclusion on the ballot “will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan,” however it does not provide concrete evidence that voters are being confused.
It’s unclear whether the new information DOJ added to its complaint will move the needle on the central legal argument that Alaska election officials are making for why the case should be dismissed. They say the law DOJ is citing – specifically the introductory text to a federal voter registration law – does not give it the right to ask a federal court to intervene in the election certification.
Ramaswamy no longer airing controversial ad featuring opponent's estranged mother
The campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, is no longer running a controversial ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent.
“It ran to completion, and we put up four other ads,” Ramaswamy said at a campaign event in Vandalia on Thursday, according to the Columbus Dispatch.
The latest version of the ad was already winding down on the air, according to AdImpact data, which shows the spot aired just twice on Wednesday.
The ad caused a national uproar when it surfaced last week. The Democratic nominee, Amy Acton, and her brother condemned the ad as a new low in the race, noting she last saw her mother when she was about 12 years old and a man her mom had married had sexually abused her.
The backlash was bipartisan. Ohio GOP Gov. Mike DeWine called on Ramaswamy to take it down. Other Ohio GOP leaders, such as Sen. Jon Husted, said it was not an ad they would have released.
After initially declining to take responsibility for the spot, Ramaswamy’s campaign confirmed it was an ad they made and doubled down on it, announcing they would spend $4 million to run it. They first aired the full 60-second spot, then switched to a 30-second version.
Kansas GOP chair says Trump's canceled rally would have energized base in a close race
President Donald Trump’s Saturday event with Sen. Roger Marshall was canceled, the RNC told the Kansas GOP this morning, but they did not give a reason, said Danedri Herbert, chairwoman of the Kansas Republican Party.
Herbert said she expected there to be some disappointment.
“This would have been a historic event for central Kansas. People’s children would remember it,” she said. “Years from now, decades from now, people would be talking about the time the president came to Salina.”
When Trump visited Kansas earlier this month, Herbert said his visit “definitely energized the base.”
“It reminded everyone that we do have a team, let’s get on the field and win something,” she said.
Earlier this year, Herbert had urged the RNC to take the Kansas senate race seriously, even before Adam Hamilton was the Democratic nominee. But her argument was not taken seriously.
“People laughed in my face. Who is laughing now?” she told CNN.
DOJ escalates fight with California election officials, issues grand jury subpoenas
The Justice Department has issued federal grand jury subpoenas to local election officials in California as part of its multi-pronged effort to prove noncitizens will vote in the upcoming elections, according to a person familiar with the matter and documents reviewed by CNN.
The subpoenas were sent to at least two employees at the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office, according to copies of the subpoenas.
The move is a significant escalation of the Justice Department’s battle with local California officials over how to identify and block what they claim are thousands of noncitizens filing ballots.
DOJ has already sued California, demanding they segregate as many as 20,000 ballots to vet voters’ citizenship.
Sent last week, the subpoenas ask for records, including their internal communications about how they would handle DOJ and Department of Homeland Security instructions to state and county officials, to be turned over to federal investigators.
The deadline to turn over those records, the subpoenas show, is two days after Election Day.
DOJ appeals California ballot segregation ruling, asks appeals court for Friday ruling
For a second time in a week, the Justice Department is launching an emergency appeal of its case seeking to segregate ballots in California, based on a controversial list of 20,000 supposed noncitizens assembled by the Trump administration.
The DOJ wants the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals to rule on the demand by Friday. It follows a Wednesday evening ruling from a district court judge that said the Trump administration had no legal right to usurp California’s ballot counting procedures.
California argues that because the ruling was a denial of a temporary restraining order, the case is not yet ripe for an appeals court to intervene. Its lawyers also told the appeals court in a Thursday letter that no briefing was required in the emergency appeal, because two of the three judges of the 9th Circuit panel overseeing the case had already indicated that, if they were to rule on the legal merits of the administration’s request, they would reject it.
The appeals court, however, has asked for a round of briefs opposing the DOJ’s request to be filed by noon ET Friday.
Meanwhile, district court Judge David Carter is moving forward with plans to investigate whether the list of alleged noncitizens the administration is citing is based on reliable data. He said Friday that he was appointing a cybersecurity expert as a so-called special master – a court appointed expert – to lead that review. There will be a hearing on Friday, November 13.
Trump explains decision to scrap Kansas rally — and lashes out when asked about his health
President Donald Trump said Thursday his decision to scrap a planned rally in Kansas this weekend had nothing to do with Sen. Roger Marshall’s electoral prospects — or his own stamina after a month of nonstop travel.
“I’m not going to Kansas because he’s doing very well,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews after arriving back from a campaign stop in South Carolina.
Trump had been scheduled to rally in Salina with Marshall, the incumbent Republican who polls show is in an unexpectedly tight race. Instead, he said he’s going to do a telerally.
But when a reporter asked Trump about his health and followed up with a question about whether the cancelation was because he was sick of traveling, Trump lashed out.
“The reason is, I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas. I’m going to Florida tomorrow, and I’ll do — if something else comes up,” he said. “But he said, ‘You’re not going to Kansas, sir. Are you feeling well?’ You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect.”
The reporter, Trump seethed, was “disgusting.”
“Put yourself in shape,” he snapped. “You look like hell.”
Trump has been campaigning nearly every day this month as he works to shore up support for Republicans. At some recent events, he has acknowledged his voice sounds hoarse after the intense bout of travel.
The Republican National Committee told the Kansas GOP this morning that the event was canceled but they did not give a reason, according to Danedri Herbert, who is the chairwoman of the Kansas Republican Party. Herbert said that she expected there to be some disappointment and that Trump’s visit to the state earlier this month “definitely energized the base.”
A spokesperson for Marshall did not respond to questions about the canceled visit.
This post has been updated with additional reporting.
No, voting machines aren't "flipping" votes
Claims of voting machines “flipping” votes are spreading online. CNN’s Gabe Cohen explains what’s behind them and how voters can check that their ballots reflect their choices.
Alaska GOP Senate candidate spotlights election recruitment controversy in new video
Incumbent GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is seizing on The New York Times report alleging that Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting a Senate candidate who shares his name, releasing a new video on the matter on social media.
The video details the reported effort, highlighting Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s former campaign manager saying that while Peltola wasn’t directly involved, she was “definitely aware.”
It also includes footage of Peltola addressing speculation about the other Dan Sullivan at a debate earlier this month, saying, “I think that Alaskans have had it up to here with the lying and the dishonesty.”
Peltola’s campaign and Democratic leadership have denied involvement.
The report has roiled the Senate battleground race, with less than a week until Election Day. The Justice Department is now dramatically accelerating its criminal probe into the ballot controversy, as the state’s governor and GOP-led House Oversight Committee open investigations.
Early voting in Georgia passes previous midterm record
Early voting in the Peach State has shattered the midterm in-person early voting record set in 2022.
Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger announced that as of 1:35 PM today, 2,294,275 Georgians had already cast their ballots during the early voting period. He also said that 108,251 absentee ballots had been accepted as of this afternoon.
“Georgians continue to head to the polls in record numbers because they trust the system,” Raffensperger said.
Early voting in Georgia is scheduled to wrap up when the polls close at 7pm Friday.
Democrats see more signs for optimism in quest to seize a majority. Catch up here
The forecaster “Inside Elections” made dozens of changes to its race ratings this week, and they favored one party by a crushing margin. Out of 64 rating changes, 63 moved toward Democrats and just one moved in the GOP’s favor.
It’s the latest of several optimistic signs for Democratic chances of seizing a majority in Congress. New CNN/SSRS polls released today showed the party strongly positioned in Michigan and Texas Senate races, and locked in tight races for GOP-held seats in Maine and Kansas.
As the grim signals stretch into areas Republicans once thought safe, President Donald Trump is racing to rallies across the country in an effort to shore up support. His stops include deep-red areas he carried easily in 2024, like South Carolina, where he delivered remarks this afternoon.
Here’s what we heard from Trump and more news from the trail today:
- Trump slammed recent polling as “totally phony” and dubbed Black and Jewish voters supporting Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed “crazy” at his rally Thursday. The president’s calls add to a cacophony of attacks on the candidate related to his Muslim faith.

Several battleground states will see a $19.2 million effort to turn voters out to the polls thanks to a Democratic group seeking to support “historically disenfranchised” voters. Vice President JD Vance announced Thursday that the Justice Department will investigate unsolicited pamphlets mailed to Texas households this month that offered resources to transgender and LGBTQ students — pamphlets that have come under fire from Democrats and a transgender group for their unknown origins.
“Now I actually at an earlier event was talking to a mom who told me, and I was shocked by it, we’re actually going to have the Department of Justice investigate, that her 11-year-old child got a letter encouraging that child to transition to a different gender,” Vance told a crowd in Texas while stumping for Republican Ken Paxton.

It’s unclear what specific letter Vance was referring to, but there’s been an ongoing controversy in Texas over pamphlets that match the general description. Those began arriving in mailboxes across Texas around October 17, just two days before early voting began, and read “TEXAS TRANS & LGBTQ+ STUDENT RESOURCE GUIDE” in bold.
They were addressed to the student at each household, CNN reported earlier this month. Another section urged readers to “Begin your journey” “with an organization trusted by students.” The situation set off a firestorm on social media as parents voiced outrage that children were receiving the material.
The Transgender Education Network of Texas, the nonprofit whose name appears throughout the brochure, has forcefully denied creating or mailing it. A former assistant attorney general in Paxton’s office, Chris Hilton, is an attorney for the LLC connected to the flyers. Critics have argued it was a move to trigger conservative voters and drive them to the polls in a tight election.
A civil court judge in Texas has ruled TENT can subpoena two LLCs to find out who is behind the flyers and text messages.

Alaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan blamed Democratic opponent Mary Peltola and her campaign for a building controversy in the race that could decide the balance of power in the Senate, saying she put another candidate also named Dan Sullivan on the ballot to trick Alaskans.
The criticism comes as the Justice Department has accelerated a criminal probe into whether Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting a Senate candidate intended to siphon votes from the incumbent, after a report by The New York Times described an alleged coordinated effort by Peltola’s campaign.
“It’s stunning the extent to which this shows contempt for the people of Alaska, and how they will do anything to get power,” the senator told Fox News on Thursday.
Although the legality of the alleged move remains unclear, Sullivan said, “the fitness for office is front and center.”
Sullivan said both Democrats and Republicans alike have contacted him expressing disgust about the controversy, which he called a “national scandal” given the race’s importance.
CNN’s Hannah Rabinowitz, Evan Perez and Tierney Sneed contributed to this post.

"The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent’s support and help catapult the Democrat to victory."

The operation began in the summer of 2025 to lure potential spoiler candidates onto the state’s unusual four-person ballot, Ms. Rios said. Mr. Kurtz, a native of Ohio, was introduced as a specialist in secret ballot maneuvers, Ms. Rios said.
Months later, in early 2026, Mr. Kurtz participated in a video call with members of the ballot composition team, Ms. Rios said. He told the group he had made contact with one of the Dan Sullivans. This Mr. Sullivan lived in the tiny village of Petersburg, and Mr. Kurtz described him as amenable to running if it would help Ms. Peltola, Ms. Rios said.
Mr. Kurtz “told us when he found him,” she said. He said Mr. Sullivan “said he hated Trump, and if it was going to help Mary, he liked Mary. He didn’t have any interest in being a politician, but if this could help.
Sullivan, the ghost candidate, claims he didn't know of the scheme and entered the race of his own accord. Meanwhile, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) was hip deep in the conspiracy.
"Text messages viewed by The Times show officials with the D.S.C.C. and the Peltola campaign communicating for months about the project," The New York Times reports. "Mr. [Anton] McParland asked for updates from 'Jarid,' 'Jared' or 'our friend,' and D.S.C.C. officials quickly scheduled calls, the messages showed."
Related: You're Not Scared Enough About the Left's Agenda If It Wins in 2026 and 2028
Trump sic'ed the Justice Department on the campaign by filing suit to block certification of the vote if the incumbent Senator Sullivan doesn't win. This has no chance whatsoever of succeeding, given the election hasn't even been held yet.
A better bet is the criminal investigation into Peltola's campaign ordered by Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy. While the intent to defraud voters is obvious, proving it in court is another question.
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” he said in a post on X. “Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.”
They may get some campaign advisors on a conspiracy charge, but that, too, is hard to prove. Perhaps it's enough that the scheme gets the widest possible exposure so that Alaska voters are fully informed before the Tuesday vote.
The huge advantage to this skullduggery by Democrats is that Alaska is a ranked-choice state. Essentially, they keep counting until someone has a majority. The other Sullivan and the other GOP candidate recruited by the Peltola campaign could siphon off enough votes to deny the incumbent a majority.

By SUZANNE DOWNING
Oct. 28, 2026 – Gov. Mike Dunleavy on Wednesday directed the Alaska Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the candidate recruitment operation exposed by The New York Times violated state law and warrants criminal charges or civil action.
The announcement opens a new state investigative front in the controversy surrounding efforts to place another Dan Sullivan on Alaska’s Senate ballot to draw votes away from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
“Today’s New York Times reporting reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates—including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator—to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes,” Dunleavy wrote on Facebook.
Breaking: New York Times investigation ties Mary Peltola to Decoy Dan recruitment
The governor said the Alaska Division of Elections investigated those concerns in June.
“The new reporting substantially supports the Division’s findings,” he wrote.
Dunleavy then announced the next step:
“I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted. The evidence will determine what happens next.”
The directive follows the Times’ investigation into what participants reportedly called a “ballot composition project.”
The newspaper described efforts involving Mary Peltola’s campaign advisers, Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee staff and lawyers to recruit candidates who could dilute Sullivan’s support.
The most conspicuous recruit was Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg, a retired teacher known to Alaska Story readers as “Decoy Dan.” He is on the general election ballot alongside the incumbent, Peltola and Gerald Heikes.
According to the Times, the operation began with instructions to search voter records for Alaskans named Dan Sullivan. Its reporting drew on interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign.
The newspaper also described recruitment efforts involving other potential candidates and pressure on Democrat David Leslie to withdraw, which opened a general election ballot position for Heikes.
Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied participating in the recruitment effort. The Petersburg Sullivan has maintained that he entered the race independently, however his claim appears weak due to several coincidences, including the fact that Peltola visited Petersburg just before he filed for office.
The governor’s announcement shifts attention from the political fallout to whether investigators can establish violations of Alaska law.
“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support,” Dunleavy wrote. “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections.”
The state investigation comes alongside a separate Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification if the incumbent Sullivan loses by a margin smaller than the votes received by the Petersburg Sullivan.
The Alaska Supreme Court previously allowed the Petersburg candidate to remain on the ballot. That eligibility decision is different from the question Dunleavy has now directed investigators to examine: whether conduct surrounding the recruitment operation violated state law.
Dunleavy closed his announcement with a warning that accountability could extend beyond individual participants.
“Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.”
